articles.title: A weekly edition, starting small
body: The Mallacoota Mouth stopped, and nothing took its place. This is a first attempt at something weekly again — smaller, and put together differently.

Approved contributors will be able to submit directly, under the headings the Mouth used. What arrives by the end of the week becomes that week's edition, and a printable copy with a table of contents.
It starts with almost nothing in it. That is the honest place to start.

articles.title: Old Mouth editions wanted
body: Thirty-seven issues are catalogued so far, covering 2020 to 2023. Issues 1772 to 1791, 1812 to 1820, and 1835 are missing, along with everything before 1771 and after 1837.
If you have old editions, or know who holds a larger collection, please get in touch through the archive page.

articles.title: From the mud of the Barwon to the quiet of Mallacoota: Frank Stokes’ deep-water days

subject.name: Frank Stokes
subject.note: Frank supplied the source material for this story and agreed to it being published.

body: Long-time Mallacoota local Frank Stokes, now 87 and enjoying a well-earned retirement in town, has plenty of stories — but not everyone knows about his high-stakes days as a commercial diver helping build Victoria’s early communications backbone.

Before tackling the treacherous coastal estuaries, Frank’s underwater skills were already well proven closer to home in East Gippsland, where he suited up to lay the critical PMG telephone cable crossing beneath the swift currents of the Snowy River at Orbost.

By late summer 1968, Frank — then 29 — took that hard-won river experience to an even bigger challenge: joining an elite eight-man crew from the Postmaster-General’s Department Mechanical Aids division for a pioneering engineering feat across the Barwon River to connect Barwon Heads and Ocean Grove.

Billed at the time as a first of its kind in the state, the Barwon project required laying more than 2,000 yards of four-inch polythene piping into a four-foot trench dug directly into the riverbed. While heavy machinery, bulldozers and an ex-US Marines amphibious “Buffalo” landing craft tackled the surface, Frank geared up with his aqualung to handle the critical inspections in the murky depths below.

Working underwater meant battling thick, vile-smelling black mud, zero visibility, and brutal tidal swings fluctuating up to nine feet between low and flood tides. Excavations could only happen during narrow windows at the dead low ebb. Submerged in the channel, Frank guided the sinking pipe sections — flooded with water, weighted down with heavy-duty chains, and welded together on the surface — ensuring the conduit settled cleanly into the river floor.
On the surface, the crew contended with snakes and rats in the mangrove swamps, but beneath the waterline it came down to Frank’s nerve and skill to make sure the 99-year-guaranteed pipe sat true.

The successful crossings at both the Snowy and the Barwon paved the way for modern automatic telephone exchanges across regional Victoria. The next time you run into Frank around Mallacoota, ask him about diving the Snowy or the Barwon back in the day — just be prepared to hear how tough underwater line-laying used to be.

articles.title: Contributors: a little formatting is now allowed
body: Text submitted to the edition stays plain by default, but four things now render: **bold**, *italic*, [links](https://lovemallacoota.au/archive.html), and bullet lists.

- Start a line with a dash for a bullet
- Leave a blank line between paragraphs
- Anything else, including HTML, appears exactly as typed
That last rule is the point. A pasted <script> tag or an onclick attribute is shown as text rather than run, so a contributor cannot change how the page behaves.

articles.title: Family notices
body: Notices are published as the family sends them. There is no charge, and there never will be.

To place one, use the submission form or speak to us directly. We will not print a name until someone in the family has asked us to, and every notice needs a contact we can reach in case we have a question.

articles.title: Ninety years, and about seventy people to mark it

subject.name: Shirley Dixon
subject.note: Written and published by her son. The family supplied the photographs.

body: Around seventy locals, friends and family gathered at Karbeethong Lodge on 25 July for Shirley's ninetieth birthday.

It was an afternoon of the ordinary and best kind — people who have known each other a long time, in a room with a view of the lake, catching up and telling stories. Ninety years is a long time to be part of a place, and a good many of the people there were in the stories being told.
The afternoon's standout was an original birthday song, written and produced for Shirley by her son Colin. It raised smiles and a few tears, which is about the right response.
You can [listen to the birthday song on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wITs63Cx9AQ), and there is a [gallery of the afternoon](https://celebrate.oze.au/shirley90/) with pictures of the day.
Happy ninetieth, Shirley — from all of us.
